newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil telecom bill welcome, but short on detail.
newsitem.headline: Brazil telecom bill welcome, but short on detail.

text.p: Brazil's new general telecommunications bill is a major step forward in opening up the country's massive telecom sector, but it fails to define important aspects of the privatization process, experts said.
Analysts said that, while satisfied that the 200-page document was finally sent to Congress Thursday, it lacked specifics about future rates policy and the sale of telecom giant Telebras.
"It shows the process is underway," said Sergio Misima, a telecom analyst with Fator Securities. "The market has been waiting for this."

The long-awaited bill was hand-delivered to Congress by Communications Minister Sergio Motta, who told reporters it will enable the government to begin "as soon as possible" the privatization of the sector.
Analysts said a preliminary reading of the bill revealed no major surprises, particularly as the government last week floated an old draft of the bill, presumably to gauge public reaction.
But the fact that the government's intentions for the sector are now in print and the document is in the hands of lawmakers was a positive sign, they said.
"All of our expectations are being confirmed and that is good," said Maxim Medvedovsky of Banco Icatu.
"Before the market was just speculating and now it is down on paper that the government indeed wants to privatize."
Analysts said the bill lacks a chronology for a new rate rebalancing and sale of Telebras, as well as the details of its break-up. But some said that was understandable.
"It's difficult for the government to set down in a law when it will do these things," Medvedovsky said. "But it is making very clear its intention to do so."
He added the law appears to leave open a range of options for the government on privatization and other issues.
Analysts said the government's plans to drive the bill through Congress by February 1 was overly optimistic, although they agreed it was likely to be approved before the end of the first quarter.
Once approved, the law would authorize the government to restructure and sell off Telebras' holding company, its long-distance unit Embratel and its 27 local operating subsidiaries.

It also would set broad policy outlines for a competitive, private telecom sector and create a regulatory watchdog under the control of the government but independent of firms operating telecom services.
The regulator, modeled on the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC), would set rates and grant maximum 20-year operating concessions, renewable for a maximum 20 years.

One analyst said he was troubled by the fact that the law appears to offer initial concessions for only eight years. "That in my view is a negative point. I didn't like seeing that," said Jacopo Valentino of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
